prize_parts.citation: for explaining how collateral constraints and financial frictions amplify macroeconomic fluctuations

statement.case_for: My configuration has not changed. B031 identifies a mature and enduring contribution: collateral constraints and financial frictions provide structural mechanisms through which balance sheets propagate and amplify aggregate disturbances. Kiyotaki and Moore are central to the collateral mechanism, while Gertler is a defensible recipient for the connected financial-accelerator contribution. The citation is deliberately limited to macroeconomic amplification, rather than purporting to credit the laureates for all macro-finance or credit-cycle research. Under that scope, the achievement has exceptional theoretical durability and sustained relevance for macroeconomic analysis.
statement.case_against: The configuration remains vulnerable because the collateral-cycle and financial-accelerator strands arose in distinct papers and coauthor constellations. A joint award can therefore obscure differences in intellectual origin or omit important contributors. B020 offers a comparably mature alternative with a clearer central originator, although its proposed three-person formulation has its own unresolved boundary between the canonical model and a wider research programme.

responses.point: Boppart argues that B031 combines related mechanisms developed in distinct papers and coauthor groupings, making both the common achievement and attribution difficult.
responses.response: I agree that this is the decisive objection and have retained a narrow formulation for that reason. The award should not describe a general theory of financial crises or the whole macro-finance literature. Its defensible common content is the demonstration that collateral and financial conditions can amplify macroeconomic shocks; Kiyotaki, Moore, and Gertler make distinct but closely connected contributions to that defined insight. The residual attribution difficulty is real, but not sufficient to outweigh the maturity and explanatory force of the bounded contribution.

responses.point: Hassler favors B020, while recognizing that its three-person allocation is contestable between a Melitz-centered canonical model and a broader heterogeneous-firm programme.
responses.response: I agree that B020 is an outstanding alternative and that Melitz is the unmistakable center of its canonical framework. That very fact sharpens the question whether Helpman and Redding should share an award for the stated achievement. B031 also requires careful delimitation, but its three credited scholars can be linked by the common issue of amplification through collateral and financial frictions. On balance I continue to prefer that mature macroeconomic mechanism, while treating B020 as the strongest alternative.

responses.point: Strömberg argues that the complementary collateral and financial-friction mechanisms form a coherent macro-finance contribution if the citation avoids claiming credit for all credit-cycle research.
responses.response: I agree. This supports retaining the three-person configuration, but only with wording that distinguishes the shared amplification insight from adjacent mechanisms and from the broader financial-accelerator literature. It also explains why I do not expand the citation beyond its precise macroeconomic claim.

uncertainties: Whether the common amplification insight is sufficiently narrow to justify joining the collateral-cycle and financial-accelerator strands in one award.
Whether an omitted contributor would be indispensable even under the restricted citation.
Whether B020's attribution issue is better resolved by a Melitz-only formulation than by its proposed broader three-person programme.
statement.conflict_note: The supplied profile records long-term coauthorship with committee chair John Hassler and several papers with committee member Timo Boppart. It identifies no professional relationship with the proposed B031 laureates; these committee-member relationships are disclosed for transparency.
